#### Independent Work.

Independently, Le Gall [LeGall24] also obtained bounds on rectangular matrix multiplication, improving over [legallrect2]. His method generalizes the approach of [duan2023] to rectangular matrices. For technical reasons, the bound on $\omega$ produced by his method does not match the bound in [duan2023]. In comparison, our method is not only a generalization of [duan2023] to rectangular matrices, but also an improvement. As a result, our bounds are better than the bounds in [LeGall24].

## 2 Technical Overview

### 2.1 Overview of Previous Work

For positive integers $a,b,c$ , the $a\times b\times c$ matrix multiplication tensor $\langle a,b,c\rangle$ is a tensor over the variable sets $\{x_{ij}\}_{i\in[a],j\in[b]},\{y_{jk}\}_{j\in[b],k\in[c]},\{z_{ki}\}_{k\in[c],i\in[a]}$ defined as the tensor computing the $a\times c$ product matrix $\{z_{ki}\}_{k\in[c],i\in[a]}$ of an $a\times b$ matrix $\{x_{ij}\}_{i\in[a],j\in[b]}$ and a $b\times c$ matrix $\{y_{jk}\}_{j\in[b],k\in[c]}$ .11 1 For integer $n\geq 0$ , the notation $[n]$ denotes $\{1,\dots,n\}$ . Specifically, $\langle a,b,c\rangle$ can be written as the following trilinear form

$$ \langle a,b,c\rangle=\sum_{i\in[a]}\sum_{j\in[b]}\sum_{k\in[c]}x_{ij}y_{jk}z_{ki}. $$

It is not hard to check that $\langle a,b,c\rangle\otimes\langle d,e,f\rangle=\langle ad,be,cf\rangle$ . For a tensor $T$ , let $R(T)$ denote the tensor rank of $T$ and the matrix multiplication exponent $\omega$ is defined as

$$ \omega\coloneqq\inf_{q\in\mathbb{N},\,q\geq 2}\log_{q}R(\langle q,q,q\rangle). $$

It is hard to directly bound the tensor rank of $\langle q,q,q\rangle$ in general, so current approaches to bounding $\omega$ utilize Schönhage’s asymptotic sum inequality [Schonhage81], which states that if one can bound the asymptotic rank of a direct sum of matrix multiplication tensors, where the asymptotic rank $\widetilde{R}(T)$ of a tensor $T$ is defined as

$$ \widetilde{R}(T)\coloneqq\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}R(T^{\otimes n})^{1/n}, $$

then one can get a bound on $\omega$ . More specifically, we recall the asymptotic sum inequality as follows.

#### Theorem 2.1 (Asymptotic Sum Inequality [Schonhage81]).

For positive integers $r>m$ and $a_{i},b_{i},c_{i}$ for $i\in[m]$ , if

$$ \widetilde{R}\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}\langle a_{i},b_{i},c_{i}\rangle\right)\leq r, $$

then $\omega\leq 3\tau$ where $\tau\in[2/3,1]$ is the solution to the equation

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{m}(a_{i}\cdot b_{i}\cdot c_{i})^{\tau}=r. $$

Schönhage’s asymptotic sum inequality gave rise to the following approach to bounding $\omega$ : start with a tensor $T$ whose asymptotic rank $\widetilde{R}(T)$ is easy to bound. Consider $T^{\otimes n}$ for some $n$ sufficiently large and we want to transform $T^{\otimes n}$ into a direct sum of matrix multiplication tensors whose asymptotic rank is upper bounded by the asymptotic rank of $\widetilde{R}(T^{\otimes n})=\widetilde{R}(T)^{n}$ . The common ways of doing such transformation is via zeroing-out, i.e., setting some variables in $T^{\otimes n}$ to zero, or the more general degeneration, whose definition is deferred to Section 3. Then we can apply the asymptotic sum inequality to get a bound on $\omega$ . Observe that if $T^{\otimes n}$ can be degenerated into $\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}\langle a_{i},b_{i},c_{i}\rangle$ , then for a fixed $\tau$ , we want to maximize the value of $\sum_{i=1}^{m}(a_{i}\cdot b_{i}\cdot c_{i})^{\tau}$ . This gives a notion of the “matrix multiplication value” of a tensor $T$ that we want to maximize. Then notice that a lower bound on the value of $T^{\otimes n}$ would directly imply an upper bound on $\omega$ via the asymptotic sum inequality. It still remains unknown how to get the best possible bound on $\omega$ via a tensor power $T^{\otimes n}$ , but the laser method provides one way to give a nontrivial bound.

#### Laser method.

Let $T$ be a tensor over three sets of variables $X,Y,Z$ . For positive integers $s_{X},s_{Y},s_{Z}$ , let $X=\bigsqcup_{i\in[s_{X}]}X_{i},Y=\bigsqcup_{j\in[s_{Y}]}Y_{j}$ and $Z=\bigsqcup_{k\in[s_{Z}]}Z_{k}$ be partitions of the $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variable sets into $s_{X},s_{Y},s_{Z}$ parts respectively. Then $T$ can be written as a sum of subtensors $\sum_{i,j,k}T_{i,j,k}$ , where $T_{i,j,k}$ denotes the subtensor of $T$ restricted to variables $X_{i},Y_{j},Z_{k}$ .

Suppose for now that each subtensor $T_{i,j,k}$ is a matrix multiplication tensor. If $T$ is a direct sum of matrix multiplication tensors, then we can apply Schönhage’s asymptotic sum inequality [Schonhage81] to obtain a bound on $\omega$ . However, $T$ is a sum of $T_{i,j,k}$ , not necessarily a direct sum.

The laser method [laser] is devised to overcome this issue. First, we take the $n$ -th tensor power of $T$ for some large $n$ , which is a tensor over variables $X^{n},Y^{n},Z^{n}$ :

$$ T^{\otimes n}=\sum_{I\in[s_{X}]^{n}}\sum_{J\in[s_{Y}]^{n}}\sum_{K\in[s_{Z}]^{n}}T_{I,J,K}, $$

where

$$ T_{I,J,K}=T_{I_{1},J_{1},K_{1}}\otimes T_{I_{2},J_{2},K_{2}}\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{I_{n},J_{n},K_{n}}. $$

We will refer to these three sets of variables as $X$ -variables, $Y$ -variables and $Z$ -variables respectively. Because each $T_{i,j,k}$ is a matrix multiplication tensor and the tensor products of several $T_{i,j,k}$ ’s will still be matrix multiplication tensors, $T_{I,J,K}$ is a matrix multiplication tensor for any $I\in[s_{X}]^{n},J\in[s_{Y}]^{n},K\in[s_{Z}]^{n}$ . For any $I\in[s_{X}]^{n}$ , let $X_{I}$ denote $X_{I_{1}}\times X_{I_{2}}\times\cdots\times X_{I_{n}}$ , which is a subset of $X^{n}$ . Similarly we define $Y_{J}$ and $Z_{K}$ . It is not difficult to see that $T_{I,J,K}$ is exactly the subtensor of $T^{\otimes n}$ when restricted to $X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K}$ . We call such subsets $X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K}$ variable blocks.

The goal of the laser method is to select some of the variable blocks $X_{I},Y_{J}$ or $Z_{K}$ and zero out all of the variables in these blocks, i.e. “zero out the blocks”, so that the remaining tensor is a direct sum of $T_{I,J,K}$ ’s.

The laser method specifies a distribution $\alpha$ over triples $(i,j,k)$ where $i\in[s_{X}],j\in[s_{Y}],k\in[s_{Z}]$ , so that for each $T_{I,J,K}$ that we want to keep in the direct sum, we require that

$$ \big|\{t\in[n]\mid(I_{t},J_{t},K_{t})=(i,j,k)\}\big|=\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot n. $$

If a subtensor $T_{I,J,K}$ satisfies (1), we say that it is consistent with the distribution $\alpha$ .

The distribution $\alpha$ induces the marginal distributions $\alpha_{X},\alpha_{Y},\alpha_{Z}$ on the $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variables over the indices $[s_{X}],[s_{Y}],[s_{Z}]$ respectively as follows. Let $\alpha_{X}$ , $\alpha_{Y}$ , $\alpha_{Z}$ be the marginal distributions of $\alpha$ on the three dimensions respectively, i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{X}(i) \displaystyle=\sum_{j\in[s_{Y}],k\in[s_{Z}]}\alpha(i,j,k)\quad\forall i\in[s_{X}], \displaystyle\alpha_{Y}(j) \displaystyle=\sum_{i\in[s_{X}],k\in[s_{Z}]}\alpha(i,j,k)\quad\forall j\in[s_{Y}], \displaystyle\alpha_{Z}(k) \displaystyle=\sum_{i\in[s_{X}],j\in[s_{Y}]}\alpha(i,j,k)\quad\forall k\in[s_{Z}]. $$

In the laser method, we zero out all $X$ -variable blocks $X_{I}$ that are not consistent with $\alpha_{X}$ ( $X_{I}$ is consistent with $\alpha_{X}$ if $|\{t\in[n]:I_{t}=i\}|=\alpha_{X}(i)\cdot n$ for every $i\in[s_{X}]$ ). We similarly zero out all $Y$ -variable blocks $Y_{J}$ that are not consistent with $\alpha_{Y}$ and $Z$ -variable blocks $Z_{K}$ that are not consistent with $\alpha_{Z}$ .

At this stage, a subtensor $T_{I,J,K}$ remains if $X_{I},Y_{J}$ and $Z_{K}$ all remain. Thus, all remaining $T_{I,J,K}$ ’s are consistent with some distribution $\alpha^{\prime}$ that induces the same marginal distributions $\alpha_{X},\alpha_{Y},\alpha_{Z}$ , though $\alpha^{\prime}$ might be different from $\alpha$ . The final stages of the laser method aim to keep a collection of independent subtensors $T_{I,J,K}$ and zero out the subtensors $T_{I,J,K}$ that are consistent with a distribution $\alpha^{\prime}\neq\alpha$ , using techniques such as hashing and greedy procedures. Eventually, the laser method obtains multiple independent copies of the tensor isomorphic to:

$$ \mathcal{T}\coloneqq\bigotimes_{i,j,k}T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot n}. $$

#### The Coppersmith-Winograd tensor $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ .

Prior works [cw90, stothers, virgi12, LeGall32power, AlmanW21, duan2023] that obtained the best bounds on $\omega$ used the Coppersmith-Winograd tensor $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ and its powers as the starting tensor $T$ in the laser method. The Coppersmith-Winograd tensor $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ for a nonnegative integer $q$ is defined as

$$ \mathrm{CW}_{q}\coloneqq x_{0}y_{0}z_{q+1}+x_{0}y_{q+1}z_{0}+x_{q+1}y_{0}z_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{q}\left(x_{0}y_{i}z_{i}+x_{i}y_{0}z_{i}+x_{i}y_{i}z_{0}\right). $$

Observe that

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{q}\left(x_{0}y_{i}z_{i}+x_{i}y_{0}z_{i}+x_{i}y_{i}z_{0}\right)\equiv\langle 1,1,q\rangle+\langle q,1,1\rangle+\langle 1,q,1\rangle, $$

so $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ is the sum of six matrix multiplication tensors where the other three are copies of $\langle 1,1,1\rangle$ . Next, we describe the leveled partitions of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ and $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell}}$ that are crucial to our analysis. For simplicity, we denote $T^{(\ell)}\coloneqq\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}$ .

For $T^{(1)}=\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ , its variable sets are partitioned into three parts

$$ \displaystyle X^{(1)} \displaystyle=X^{(1)}_{0}\sqcup X^{(1)}_{1}\sqcup X^{(1)}_{2}=\{x_{0}\}\sqcup\{x_{1},\dots,x_{q}\}\sqcup\{x_{q+1}\}, \displaystyle Y^{(1)} \displaystyle=Y^{(1)}_{0}\sqcup Y^{(1)}_{1}\sqcup Y^{(1)}_{2}=\{y_{0}\}\sqcup\{y_{1},\dots,y_{q}\}\sqcup\{y_{q+1}\}, \displaystyle Z^{(1)} \displaystyle=Z^{(1)}_{0}\sqcup Z^{(1)}_{1}\sqcup Z^{(1)}_{2}=\{z_{0}\}\sqcup\{z_{1},\dots,z_{q}\}\sqcup\{z_{q+1}\}. $$

Notice that under this partition, a constituent tensor $T^{(1)}_{i,j,k}$ is nonzero if and only if $i+j+k=2$ .

For $T^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}$ with variable sets $X^{(\ell)},Y^{(\ell)},Z^{(\ell)}$ , the above partition on $T^{(1)}$ directly induces a partition on the variable sets $X^{(\ell)},Y^{(\ell)},Z^{(\ell)}$ where each part of the partition is indexed by a $\{0,1,2\}$ -sequence of length $2^{\ell-1}$ . Specifically, this gives the partition

$$ X^{(\ell)}=\bigsqcup_{(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}}X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{1}}\otimes X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{2}}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}} $$

for $X$ -variables and analogous partitions for $Y$ - and $Z$ -variables.

One can use the laser method on these partitions. However, this would not yield an improved bound on $\omega$ from what one would get just by analyzing $T^{(1)}$ . The reason behind the improvement obtained by analyzing higher powers of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ comes from the fact that we can consider the following coarsening of the above partition where the parts corresponding to sequences with the same sum are “merged” into a single part. More specifically, we have

$$ X^{(\ell)}=\bigsqcup_{i=0}^{2^{\ell}}X_{i}^{(\ell)},\qquad\textup{where}\quad X_{i}^{(\ell)}\coloneqq\bigsqcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}\\
\sum_{t}\hat{i}_{t}=i\end{subarray}}X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{1}}\otimes X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{2}}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}}. $$

We refer to this specific partition of $T^{(\ell)}$ as the level- $\ell$ partition. Note that we can also view this partition as obtained from coarsening the level-( $\ell-1$ ) partition, i.e.,

$$ X_{i}^{(\ell)}=\bigsqcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq i^{\prime}\leq i\\
0\leq i^{\prime},i-i^{\prime}\leq 2^{\ell}\end{subarray}}X^{(\ell-1)}_{i^{\prime}}\otimes X^{(\ell-1)}_{i-i^{\prime}}. $$

We can partition the variable sets $Y^{(\ell)}$ and $Z^{(\ell)}$ similarly. Then we use $T^{(\ell)}_{i,j,k}$ to denote the subtensor of $T^{(\ell)}$ restricted to the variable subsets $X_{i}^{(\ell)},Y_{j}^{(\ell)},Z_{k}^{(\ell)}$ and note that $T^{(\ell)}_{i,j,k}$ is nonzero if and only if $i+j+k=2^{\ell}$ . We call $T^{(\ell)}_{i,j,k}$ a level- $\ell$ constituent tensor, $X^{(\ell)}_{i},Y^{(\ell)}_{j},Z^{(\ell)}_{k}$ level- $\ell$ variable blocks, and we omit the superscript $(\ell)$ when $\ell$ is clear from context.

For $\ell>1$ , some level- $\ell$ constituent tensors $T^{(\ell)}_{i,j,k}$ are no longer matrix multiplication tensors, so each independent copy of $\mathcal{T}=\bigotimes_{i,j,k}\bigl(T_{i,j,k}^{(\ell)}\bigr)^{\otimes\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot n}$ may also no longer be a matrix multiplication tensor. To resolve this issue, prior works [cw90, stothers, virgi12, LeGall32power, AlmanW21] use the laser method recursively to analyze $T_{i,j,k}$ ’s that are not matrix multiplication tensors.

#### The work of [duan2023].

Consider the analysis on the tensor $T^{(\ell)}$ of the laser method. In previous approaches prior to the work of Duan, Wu and Zhou [duan2023], one would first apply the laser method on $T^{(\ell)}$ to obtain multiple copies of $\mathcal{T}=\bigotimes_{i,j,k}\bigl(T_{i,j,k}^{(\ell)}\bigr)^{\otimes\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot n}$ which consists of level- $\ell$ constituent tensors $T_{i,j,k}^{(\ell)}$ and do not share level- $\ell$ variable blocks. Then for each $T_{i,j,k}^{(\ell)}$ that is not a matrix multiplication tensor, one would recursively apply the laser method to obtain multiple copies of some other tensors that are independent over level- $(\ell-1)$ variable blocks.

Recall that for a level- $\ell$ constituent tensor $T_{i,j,k}^{(\ell)}$ , we can partition its variable set $X_{i}^{(\ell)},Y_{j}^{(\ell)},Z_{k}^{(\ell)}$ recursively into $\bigsqcup_{i^{\prime}}X_{i^{\prime}}^{(\ell-1)}\otimes X_{i-i^{\prime}}^{(\ell-1)}$ , $\bigsqcup_{j^{\prime}}Y_{j^{\prime}}^{(\ell-1)}\otimes Y_{j-j^{\prime}}^{(\ell-1)}$ and $\bigsqcup_{k^{\prime}}Z_{k^{\prime}}^{(\ell-1)}\otimes Z_{k-k^{\prime}}^{(\ell-1)}$ respectively. In the first recursive step, when applying the laser method on $T_{i,j,k}^{(\ell)}$ , we take the $n^{\prime}$ -th tensor power $\bigl(T_{i,j,k}^{(\ell)}\bigr)^{\otimes n^{\prime}}$ of $T_{i,j,k}^{(\ell)}$ for some large $n^{\prime}$ and specify a distribution $\beta$ over triples $((i^{\prime},i-i^{\prime}),\,(j^{\prime},j-j^{\prime}),\,(k^{\prime},k-k^{\prime}))$ where $0\leq i^{\prime}\leq i$ , $0\leq j^{\prime}\leq j$ , $0\leq k^{\prime}\leq k$ , and zero out all variables blocks that are not consistent with the marginal distributions induced by $\beta$ . Therefore, in $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes n^{\prime}}$ , only a subset of the level- $(\ell-1)$ variable blocks survive the above zeroing-out.

*Figure 1: High-level comparison between this work and prior works on $(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 4})^{\otimes n}$ . Here, $\alpha$ is a distribution over level- $3$ constituent tensors, $\beta$ is a collection of distributions over level- $2$ constituent tensors, and $\gamma$ is a collection of distributions over level- $1$ constituent tensors.*

Now suppose we can move the above zeroing-out step earlier, say before we have independent copies of $\mathcal{T}$ when we first apply the laser method on $T^{(\ell)}$ , then instead of keeping independent copies of $\mathcal{T}$ , we only need to keep a subtensor $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ of it, where $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ is $\mathcal{T}$ after applying the above zeroing-out step. This leads to one of the key observations in [duan2023]: we do not need to have copies of $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ that are fully independent over the level- $\ell$ variable blocks. Instead, any two copies can share the same level- $\ell$ variable block as long as they do not share the same level- $(\ell-1)$ variable blocks that would survive the first zeroing-out in the recursive application of the laser method on the level- $\ell$ constituent tensors. As a result, we can potentially keep more independent copies of $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ , because of the relaxed constraints, and each copy $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ would still be essentially as good as $\mathcal{T}$ for the purpose of the analysis because we are merely moving a later zeroing-out earlier. Because we are keeping more copies, by the asymptotic sum inequality, we will achieve a better bound for $\omega$ .

As illustrated in Fig. 1, consider $(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 4})^{\otimes n}$ and suppose $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are (collections of) distributions over level- $3$ , level- $2$ , level- $1$ constituent tensors respectively. In subfigure (a), works prior to [duan2023] including [virgi12, AlmanW21, LeGall32power] zero out level- $3$ blocks according to $\alpha$ and obtain level- $3$ -independent22 2 We say several subtensors of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes N}$ are level- $\ell$ -independent if they do not share any level- $\ell$ variable block, and thus they are also independent. copies of $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ before zeroing out level- $2$ blocks. As shown in subfigure (b), Duan et al. [duan2023] moved the step of zeroing out level- $2$ blocks according to $\beta$ earlier and only obtained level- $2$ -independence as opposed to level- $3$ -independence.

It is not obvious how one can accomplish the above modification. Duan et al. [duan2023] considered the notion of split distributions, which roughly measures how a level- $\ell$ block “splits” into level-( $\ell-1$ ) blocks with respect to the recursive leveled partition. By observing the split distribution of a level- $\ell$ block, one gains some partial information about the level- $(\ell-1)$ blocks that allows the modification of zeroing out level- $(\ell-1)$ blocks inconsistent with $\beta$ earlier. Ideally, one would hope to achieve this modification symmetrically over the $X$ -, $Y$ -, and $Z$ -variables, i.e., allow the sharing of level- $\ell$ variable blocks in all three dimensions, but the method in [duan2023] did not achieve that. Instead, their technique works when the multiple copies of $\mathcal{T}$ only share the same level- $\ell$ $Z$ -variable block while each $X$ - and $Y$ -variable block needs to be contained in a unique level- $\ell$ subtensor. (More generally, their technique works when level- $\ell$ variable blocks are shared in exactly one of $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variables). In order to set up the tensor satisfying the required constraints, they need to zero out the $Z$ -variable blocks asymmetrically with respect to the $X$ - and $Y$ -variables. It still remains an open question whether the techniques in [duan2023] can be symmetrized over the three dimensions.

Another technical detail is that the obtained independent copies of tensors in [duan2023] are not all necessarily full copies of $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ . That is, some variables of the independent tensors are zeroed out. This creates independent copies of $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ but with some “holes”. Because of the asymmetry of their method, such holes can only appear in $Z$ -variables. In order to overcome this issue, they showed that, as long as the fraction of holes is small, and all holes are in $Z$ -variables, one can degenerate a small number of independent copies of $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ with holes to a full copy of $\mathcal{T}$ . Prior to their work, Schönhage [Schonhage81] also studied this problem of degenerating multiple independent copies of a tensor with holes to a full copy of the tensor. Schönhage’s method applied to the case when two of the three dimensions can have holes, but it focuses only on matrix multiplication tensors.

### 2.2 Our Improvements

#### Complete split distribution.

We take the observation of [duan2023] one step further. The high-level idea is the following: instead of keeping copies of $\mathcal{T}$ that are independent over level- $(\ell-1)$ variable blocks, we keep copies of it that are independent over level- $1$ variable blocks. For $\ell>1$ , this should give more degrees of freedom and enable us to keep more copies of $\mathcal{T}$ . As illustrated in Fig. 1 (c), we directly move the step of zeroing out level- $1$ blocks according to $\gamma$ earlier and obtain level- $1$ independence as opposed in level- $2$ independence in [duan2023].

To implement the above idea, we utilize the notion of complete split distributions, which can be viewed as an extension of the notion of split distributions used in [duan2023]. Recall that in [duan2023], a level- $\ell$ split distribution measures how a level- $\ell$ variable block splits into level- $(\ell-1)$ blocks. A level- $\ell$ complete split distribution measures how a level- $\ell$ block splits into level- $1$ variable blocks. Specifically, a level- $1$ block sequence of length $2^{\ell-1}\cdot n$ in $T^{(\ell)}$ can be viewed as $n$ consecutive chunks of $\{0,1,2\}$ -sequences each of length $2^{\ell-1}$ , and we consider the proportion of each of these $3^{2^{\ell-1}}$ possible types of chunks in the $n$ chunks. A level- $\ell$ complete split distribution is a distribution on these $3^{2^{\ell-1}}$ types of chunks, and a level- $1$ block sequence (and its corresponding level- $1$ variable block) is said to be consistent with a level- $\ell$ complete split distribution if the proportion of each type of chunks matches the corresponding probability specified in the complete split distribution.

Let $\beta_{X},\beta_{Y},\beta_{Z}$ be three level- $\ell$ complete split distributions, and let $T_{i,j,k}$ be a level- $\ell$ constituent tensor. We will consider the tensor $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes n}[\beta_{X},\beta_{Y},\beta_{Z}]$ , which is obtained from $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes n}$ by zeroing out all level- $1$ $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variable blocks that are not consistent with $\beta_{X},\beta_{Y},\beta_{Z}$ respectively. We call this “enforcing the complete split distributions”. In our recursive steps, we will analyze $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes n}[\beta_{X},\beta_{Y},\beta_{Z}]$ instead of $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes n}$ .

#### Enforcing split distributions in all three dimensions.

Dual et al. [duan2023] only enforce their split distribution in one of the dimensions (the $Z$ variables). In our method, we need to enforce complete split distributions in all three dimensions. Here we explain why.

First of all, when analyzing a level- $\ell$ constituent tensor $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes n}$ , [duan2023] only consider split distributions, instead of complete split distributions. Every level- $(\ell-1)$ block sequence in $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes n}$ can be viewed as a length- $(2n)$ sequence on $\{0,1,\ldots,2^{\ell-1}\}$ . If we split the sequence to chunks of length $2$ , we obtain a length- $n$ sequence of pairs in $\{0,1,\ldots,2^{\ell-1}\}^{2}$ . The split distribution used in [duan2023] essentially specifies the proportion of each type of pairs, and they zero out all level- $(\ell-1)$ variable blocks that are not consistent with the specified proportions.

Similar to what we discussed earlier, when enforcing the split distribution on the tensor $T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}$ (or $T_{i-i^{\prime},j-j^{\prime},k-k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}$ ), the constraint becomes a constraint that enforces the proportion of each level- $(\ell-1)$ variable block in the level- $(\ell-1)$ variable blocks in $T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}$ . Since there is only one level- $(\ell-1)$ block in $T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}$ , either the whole tensor $T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}$ satisfies the constraints, or it does not. Thus, the constraints of the split distribution do not carry over to further recursion levels.

When analyzing each constituent tensor $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes n}$ , Duan et al. [duan2023] aim to obtain some “symmetrized value” of $T_{i,j,k}$ , similar to previous works [cw90, stothers, virgi12, LeGall32power, AlmanW21]. As a result, when analyzing $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes n}$ , they apply their method multiple times to enforce a split distribution on each of the three possible dimensions, i.e., they can choose to share $X$ -, $Y$ -, or $Z$ -variables depending on which application of their method it is. Still, the constraints of the split distribution do not carry over to the next recursion level as discussed in the previous paragraph. Thus, in their analysis, holes only appear in one of the dimensions.

However, when enforcing a complete split distribution, the constraints carry over to further recursion levels: say in the analysis for $T_{i,j,k}$ in some application of the method in the current level, we choose to enforce a complete split distribution on $Z$ -variables. This constraint still has an effect on the next level. However, in the analysis at the next level, we can choose to enforce a complete split distribution on $Y$ -variables instead. This creates constraints on the complete split distribution in two dimensions. In general, these constraints can appear in all three dimensions, and therefore, we need to handle holes in all three dimensions.

#### A technical issue.

A technical issue arises if we enforce complete split distributions in three dimensions. We consider a simplified scenario where the support of the distribution $\beta$ has size $1$ to explain the issue. In other words, we aim to zero out $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes n}$ into independent copies of $(T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}\otimes T_{i-i^{\prime},j-j^{\prime},k-k^{\prime}})^{\otimes n}$ for some $i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}$ . In this simplified scenario, if we do not enforce complete split distributions, we could rewrite $(T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}\otimes T_{i-i^{\prime},j-j^{\prime},k-k^{\prime}})^{\otimes n}$ equivalently as $T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}\otimes T_{i-i^{\prime},j-j^{\prime},k-k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}$ by simply permuting the indices, and then recursively analyze $T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}$ and $T_{i-i^{\prime},j-j^{\prime},k-k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}$ separately. Now with complete split distribution, this step becomes problematic. Suppose we are able to obtain independent copies of

$$ \mathcal{T}_{1}\coloneqq(T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}\otimes T_{i-i^{\prime},j-j^{\prime},k-k^{\prime}})^{\otimes n}\left[\beta_{X},\beta_{Y},\beta_{Z}\right], $$

for some $\beta_{X},\beta_{Y},\beta_{Z}$ . Then in order to recursively analyze $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ , we instead need a tensor

$$ \mathcal{T}_{2}\coloneqq\left(T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}\bigl[\beta_{X}^{(L)},\beta_{Y}^{(L)},\beta_{Z}^{(L)}\bigr]\right)\otimes\left(T_{i-i^{\prime},j-j^{\prime},k-k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}\bigl[\beta_{X}^{(R)},\beta_{Y}^{(R)},\beta_{Z}^{(R)}\bigr]\right), $$

for some level- $(\ell-1)$ complete split distributions $\beta_{X}^{(L)},\beta_{Y}^{(L)},\beta_{Z}^{(L)},\beta_{X}^{(R)},\beta_{Y}^{(R)},\beta_{Z}^{(R)}$ .

Let us discuss how the above level- $(\ell-1)$ complete split distributions are related to $\beta_{X},\beta_{Y},\beta_{Z}$ . To give some intuition, in each length- $2^{\ell}$ chunk of a level- $1$ block sequence in $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ , the first half-chunk belongs to some $T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}$ , and the second half-chunk belongs to some $T_{i-i^{\prime},j-j^{\prime},k-k^{\prime}}$ . In $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ , we permute the indices so that all the first half-chunks belonging to some $T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}$ are put together in the first half of the resulting sequence, and all the second half-chunks belonging to some $T_{i-i^{\prime},j-j^{\prime},k-k^{\prime}}$ are put together in the second half of the resulting sequence. If we enforce a level- $\ell$ complete split distribution $\beta_{X}$ on a level- $1$ block sequence $\hat{I}\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ in $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ , what would the permuted sequence look like? Let $\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-2}}$ denote two length- $2^{\ell-2}$ chunks and let $\sigma_{1}\circ\sigma_{2}$ denote their concatenation. Since $\hat{I}$ is consistent with $\beta_{X}$ , $\hat{I}$ contains $\beta_{X}(\sigma_{1}\circ\sigma_{2})\cdot n$ chunks $\sigma_{1}\circ\sigma_{2}$ for every $\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}$ . For each of these chunks, $\sigma_{1}$ gets permuted to the first half of the permuted level- $1$ block sequence in $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ , and $\sigma_{2}$ gets permuted to the second half of the permuted level- $1$ block sequence in $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ . Summing over all $\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}$ , it is not difficult to verify that

$$ \beta_{X}^{(L)}(\sigma_{1})=\sum_{\sigma_{2}}\beta_{X}(\sigma_{1}\circ\sigma_{2}),\qquad\beta_{X}^{(R)}(\sigma_{2})=\sum_{\sigma_{1}}\beta_{X}(\sigma_{1}\circ\sigma_{2}). $$

In this sense, $\beta_{X}^{(L)}$ and $\beta_{X}^{(R)}$ can be viewed as two marginal distributions of $\beta_{X}$ . This similarly holds for $Y$ and $Z$ .

One set of constraints we can add to make $\beta_{X}^{(L)}$ and $\beta_{X}^{(R)}$ always the two marginal distributions of $\beta_{X}$ is $\beta_{X}=\beta_{X}^{(L)}\times\beta_{X}^{(R)}$ , namely we enforce $\beta_{X}$ to be the joint distribution of (independently distributed) $\beta_{X}^{(L)}$ and $\beta_{X}^{(R)}$ . Similarly we can add the constraints $\beta_{Y}=\beta_{Y}^{(L)}\times\beta_{Y}^{(R)}$ and $\beta_{Z}=\beta_{Z}^{(L)}\times\beta_{Z}^{(R)}$ .

However, even with these constraints, $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ might not necessarily be equivalent to $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ . By the above reasoning, every level- $1$ block sequence in $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ is permuted into a level- $1$ block sequence in $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ , but not all block sequences in $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ can be obtained this way. Intuitively, this is because joint distributions can determine marginal distributions, which means that, for instance, $\beta_{X}^{(L)}\times\beta_{X}^{(R)}$ can determine both $\beta_{X}^{(L)}$ and $\beta_{X}^{(R)}$ . The other way is not true, and there could be multiple joint distributions whose marginals satisfy $\beta_{X}^{(L)}$ and $\beta_{X}^{(R)}$ .

By a careful calculation, one can still show that the proportion of $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variables in $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ that are not in $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ is at most a $1-2^{-o(N)}$ fraction of those in $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ . These variables become holes. Unfortunately, the methods in previous works [Schonhage81, duan2023] do not apply, as they are unable to fix holes that are present in all three dimensions ( $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variables).

Next, we discuss how we fix the technical issue.

#### Intuition of the fix.

The first step towards resolving this issue is to decrease the fraction of holes in all three dimensions, from $1-2^{-o(N)}$ all the way down to $2^{-\Omega(N)}$ . Then we describe a generic method adapted from [duanpersonal] for fixing holes in all three dimensions as long as the fractions of holes are small.

For the first step, we slightly relax the condition for zeroing out variables in $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ . Let $\varepsilon>0$ be an arbitrary constant. For any $T_{i,j,k}$ , we use $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes n}[\beta_{X},\beta_{Y},\beta_{Z},\varepsilon]$ to denote $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes n}$ but we zero out all level- $1$ $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variables, where the proportion of each chunk in $\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ in their level- $1$ block sequence differs at most $\varepsilon$ from the corresponding probability in $\beta_{X},\beta_{Y},\beta_{Z}$ respectively. That is, we allow some small flexibility when zeroing out variables. Then, let

$$ \mathcal{T}_{1}^{\prime}\coloneqq\bigl(T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}\otimes T_{i-i^{\prime},j-j^{\prime},k-k^{\prime}}\bigr)^{\otimes n}\left[\beta_{X}^{(L)}\times\beta_{X}^{(R)},\;\beta_{Y}^{(L)}\times\beta_{Y}^{(R)},\;\beta_{Z}^{(L)}\times\beta_{Z}^{(R)},\;\varepsilon\right], $$

and recall

$$ \mathcal{T}_{2}=\left(T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}\bigl[\beta_{X}^{(L)},\beta_{Y}^{(L)},\beta_{Z}^{(L)}\bigr]\right)\otimes\left(T_{i-i^{\prime},j-j^{\prime},k-k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}\bigl[\beta_{X}^{(R)},\beta_{Y}^{(R)},\beta_{Z}^{(R)}\bigr]\right). $$

Intuitively, we allow more flexibility in $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ than that in $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ , so that more variables remain in $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ compared to $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ , and the fraction of holes should become smaller. The idea for proving this is to use concentration bounds: if we pick a uniformly random level- $1$ $X$ -variable block from $T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}\bigl[\beta_{X}^{(L)},\beta_{Y}^{(L)},\beta_{Z}^{(L)}\bigr]$ and another uniformly random level- $1$ $X$ -variable block from $T_{i-i^{\prime},j-j^{\prime},k-k^{\prime}}^{\otimes n}\bigl[\beta_{X}^{(R)},\beta_{Y}^{(R)},\beta_{Z}^{(R)}\bigr]$ , then with very high probability ( $1-2^{-\Omega(n)}$ ), the combination (interleaving the length $2^{\ell-2}$ chunks between their level- $1$ block sequences) of them satisfies $\beta_{X}^{(L)}\times\beta_{X}^{(R)}$ , up to $\varepsilon$ additive error. Then the fraction of holes is $2^{-\Omega(n)}$ . Similar reasons also apply to $Y$ - and $Z$ -variables.

#### Fixing the holes in all three dimensions.

Suppose we have many “broken” copies of some tensor $T$ , in each of which a small fraction of variables (holes) are missing. The goal of this step is to degenerate these broken tensors into one without holes. Schönhage [Schonhage81] solved this problem for matrix multiplication tensors with holes in only $X$ - and $Y$ -variables, but not $Z$ , via an elegant linear transformation. Duan et al. [duan2023] introduced another method for so-called standard form tensors, which are quite general and are able to capture tensor products of constituent tensors, but can only deal with holes in a single dimension. Duan [duanpersonal] developed a method utilizing an elegant recursive approach for fixing holes in all three dimensions, but only for matrix multiplication tensors.

We generalize the method of [duanpersonal] so that it can fix holes in all three dimensions simultaneously, while supporting a broad class of tensors similar to [duan2023]. The only additional requirement compared to [duan2023] is that the fraction of holes is below $O(1/\log N)$ , where $N$ is the number of variables in the tensor $T$ . This requirement is satisfied via the previous step of the fix.

Next, we provide some intuition of the recursive hole-fixing approach. Assume $T$ is supported on variable sets $X,Y,Z$ , and the fraction of holes in every copy of $T$ does not exceed $c\ll 1$ . We first take one broken copy of $T$ , which we call $T_{\textup{hole}}$ , and let $X^{(0)},Y^{(0)},Z^{(0)}$ denote the set of holes in $T_{\textup{hole}}$ ; let $X^{(1)}\coloneqq X\setminus X^{(0)}$ , $Y^{(1)}\coloneqq Y\setminus Y^{(0)}$ , $Z^{(1)}\coloneqq Z\setminus Z^{(0)}$ represent the set of non-hole variables. We can further divide $T$ into the sum of eight subtensors:

$$ \displaystyle T\,=\,\sum_{a,b,c\in\{0,1\}}T\big|_{X^{(a)},Y^{(b)},Z^{(c)}}=T_{\textup{hole}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a,b,c\in\{0,1\}\\
1\in\{a,b,c\}\end{subarray}}T\big|_{X^{(a)},Y^{(b)},Z^{(c)}}, $$

where $T|_{X^{\prime},Y^{\prime},Z^{\prime}}$ denotes the subtensor of $T$ over subsets of variables $X^{\prime}\subseteq X$ , $Y^{\prime}\subseteq Y$ , and $Z^{\prime}\subseteq Z$ . We directly use the broken copy $T_{\textup{hole}}$ for the first term, and recurse into seven subproblems to produce the other terms. In each subproblem, at least one of the variable sets is $X_{1}$ , $Y_{1}$ or $Z_{1}$ , which is $c$ times the size of $X$ , $Y$ , or $Z$ . As long as $c$ is very small, the number of broken copies of $T$ used in this recursive algorithm is affordable.

#### Rectangular matrix multiplication.

In the analysis for square matrix multiplication, we could lower bound the “symmetrized value” of every constituent tensor $T_{i,j,k}$ , which captures the asymptotic ability of $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes n}\otimes T_{j,k,i}^{\otimes n}\otimes T_{k,i,j}^{\otimes n}$ to degenerate into matrix multiplication tensors. The reason why we could symmetrize the constituent tensors is that we want to obtain square matrix multiplication tensors $\left\langle a,a,a\right\rangle$ for some $a$ , which is symmetric about all three dimensions. The situation is different when we consider rectangular matrix multiplications, where we produce matrix multiplication tensors of the form $\left\langle a,a^{\kappa},a\right\rangle$ to bound $\omega(1,\kappa,1)$ . Thus, we no longer treat the analysis of each constituent tensor $T_{i,j,k}$ as an individual subproblem, because the proportion of $T_{i,j,k}$ , $T_{j,k,i}$ , and $T_{k,i,j}$ could be different. Hence, it is natural to adopt the framework introduced by Le Gall [legallrect] (and further used in [legallrect2]) for rectangular matrix multiplication: we directly apply the laser method on a tensor consisting of multiple constituent tensors, e.g., on $\mathcal{T}=\bigotimes_{i,j,k}T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot n}$ , rather than doing this for every term $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot n}$ separately.

#### Difficulty of applying the refined laser method.

Another natural attempt would be to combine our techniques with the refined laser method introduced in [AlmanW21], which aims to reduce the “penalty term” that arises when we deal with the block triples inconsistent with the selected distribution $\alpha$ but consistent with the marginals of $\alpha$ . Alman and Vassilevska W. [AlmanW21] pick a collection of disjoint level- $\ell$ block triples $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ consistent with the chosen distribution $\alpha$ , which we call the “wanted” triples. Then, they zero out a wanted triple with probability $1-p$ and keep it with probability $p$ . Any “unwanted” triple $X_{I^{\prime}}Y_{J^{\prime}}Z_{K^{\prime}}$ only remains with probability $p^{3}$ , since three involved variable blocks come from three different wanted triples and are zeroed out independently; in contrast, every wanted triple has probability $p$ to remain. The gap between $p$ and $p^{3}$ makes it a nontrivial improvement beyond the older method (increasing the modulus of hashing, see, e.g., [stothers, virgi12, LeGall32power]), which produces a gap between $p$ and $p^{2}$ .

However, a difficulty arises when the refined laser method is combined with the asymmetric hashing technique in [duan2023] and this paper. Since we allow, e.g., level- $\ell$ $Z$ -variable blocks to be shared, we can no longer zero out all three blocks $X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K}$ when we decide to give up on this triple, as $Z_{K}$ might be utilized by other wanted triples. If we only zero out $X_{I}$ and $Y_{J}$ simultaneously, the probability of remaining becomes $p$ (for a wanted triple) versus $p^{2}$ (for an unwanted triple), which results in the same bound as the older approach.

## 3 Preliminaries

### 3.1 Tensors and Tensor Operations

#### Tensors.

A tensor $T$ over variable sets $X=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{|X|}\}$ , $Y=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{|Y|}\}$ , $Z=\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{|Z|}\}$ and field $\mathbb{F}$ is a trilinear form

$$ T=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}a_{i,j,k}\cdot x_{i}y_{j}z_{k}, $$

where all $a_{i,j,k}$ are from $\mathbb{F}$ . $X,Y,Z$ are also called the support of the tensor. If all $a_{i,j,k}\in\{0,1\}$ , the tensor $T$ can be considered as over any field $\mathbb{F}$ , which is the case for all tensors involved in this paper.

In the following, assume $T$ is a tensor over $X=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{|X|}\}$ , $Y=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{|Y|}\}$ , $Z=\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{|Z|}\}$ and $T^{\prime}$ is a tensor over $X^{\prime}=\{x^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,x^{\prime}_{|X^{\prime}|}\}$ , $Y^{\prime}=\{y^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,y^{\prime}_{|Y^{\prime}|}\}$ , $Z^{\prime}=\{z^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,z^{\prime}_{|Z^{\prime}|}\}$ , written as

$$ T=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}a_{i,j,k}\cdot x_{i}y_{j}z_{k},\qquad T^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{|X^{\prime}|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y^{\prime}|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z^{\prime}|}b_{i,j,k}\cdot x^{\prime}_{i}y^{\prime}_{j}z^{\prime}_{k}, $$

#### Tensor Operations.

Recall the following tensor operations between two tensors $T$ and $T^{\prime}$ :

- • The sum $T+T^{\prime}$ is only defined when both tensors are supported on the same sets $(X,Y,Z)=(X^{\prime},Y^{\prime},Z^{\prime})$ , given by

$$ T+T^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}(a_{i,j,k}+b_{i,j,k})\cdot x_{i}y_{j}z_{k}. $$

- • The direct sum $T\oplus T^{\prime}$ equals the sum $T+T^{\prime}$ over disjoint unions $X\sqcup X^{\prime}$ , $Y\sqcup Y^{\prime}$ , and $Z\sqcup Z^{\prime}$ , i.e., we first relabel the variables so that $T$ and $T^{\prime}$ have disjoint supports, and then take their sum. If $T$ and $T^{\prime}$ are supported on disjoint variable sets, their sum is the same as their direct sum, in which case we say $T$ and $T^{\prime}$ are independent. We write $T^{\oplus n}\coloneqq\underbrace{T\oplus T\oplus\cdots\oplus T}_{n~\textup{copies}}$ to denote the sum of $n$ independent copies of $T$ .

- • The tensor product, a.k.a. the Kronecker product, is defined as the tensor

$$ T\otimes T^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}\sum_{i^{\prime}=1}^{|X^{\prime}|}\sum_{j^{\prime}=1}^{|Y^{\prime}|}\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{|Z^{\prime}|}a_{i,j,k}\cdot b_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}\cdot(x_{i},x^{\prime}_{i^{\prime}})\cdot(y_{j},y^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}})\cdot(z_{k},z^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}}) $$

over variable sets $X\times X^{\prime}$ , $Y\times Y^{\prime}$ , and $Z\times Z^{\prime}$ . We write $T^{\otimes n}\coloneqq\underbrace{T\otimes T\otimes\cdots\otimes T}_{n~\textup{times}}$ to denote the $n$ -th tensor power of $T$ .

- • We say $T$ and $T^{\prime}$ are isomorphic, denoted by $T\equiv T^{\prime}$ , if $|X|=|X^{\prime}|$ , $|Y|=|Y^{\prime}|$ , $|Z|=|Z^{\prime}|$ , and there are permutations $\pi_{X},\pi_{Y},\pi_{Z}$ over $[|X|],[|Y|],[|Z|]$ respectively, such that $a_{i,j,k}=b_{\pi_{X}(i),\pi_{Y}(j),\pi_{Z}(k)}$ for all $i,j,k$ . In other words, both tensors are equivalent up to a relabeling of the variables.

### 3.2 Tensor Rank

Given a tensor $T$ over $X,Y,Z$ , the tensor rank $R(T)$ is defined to be the minimum integer $r\geq 0$ such that $T$ can be written as

$$ T=\sum_{t=1}^{r}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}a_{t,i}\cdot x_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}b_{t,j}\cdot y_{j}\right)\left(\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}c_{t,k}\cdot z_{k}\right), $$

where the above sum is called the rank decomposition of $T$ .

Given two tensors $T,T^{\prime}$ , the tensor rank satisfies the following property with respect to tensor operations.

- • $R(T+T^{\prime})\leq R(T)+R(T^{\prime})$ .

- • $R(T\oplus T^{\prime})\leq R(T)+R(T^{\prime})$ .

- • $R(T\otimes T^{\prime})\leq R(T)\cdot R(T^{\prime}).$

The asymptotic rank $\tilde{R}(T)$ of $T$ is defined as

$$ \tilde{R}(T):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(R(T^{\otimes n})\right)^{1/n}. $$

Due to the third item above and Fekete’s lemma, the asymptotic rank is well-defined and upper bounded by $R(T^{\otimes m})^{1/m}$ for any fixed integer $m>0$ .

### 3.3 Degenerations, Restrictions, Zero-outs

Let $T$ be a tensor over $X,Y,Z$ and $T^{\prime}$ be a tensor over $X^{\prime},Y^{\prime},Z^{\prime}$ . Both $T$ and $T^{\prime}$ are tensors over a field $\mathbb{F}$ .

#### Degeneration.

Let $\mathbb{F}[\lambda]$ be the ring of polynomials of the formal variable $\lambda$ . We say that $T^{\prime}$ is a degeneration of $T$ , written as $T\unrhd T^{\prime}$ , if there exists $\mathbb{F}[\lambda]$ -linear maps

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{X} \displaystyle:\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}[\lambda]}(X)\to\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}[\lambda]}(X^{\prime}), \displaystyle\phi_{Y} \displaystyle:\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}[\lambda]}(Y)\to\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}[\lambda]}(Y^{\prime}), \displaystyle\phi_{Z} \displaystyle:\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}[\lambda]}(Z)\to\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}[\lambda]}(Z^{\prime}), $$

and $d\in\mathbb{N}$ such that

$$ T^{\prime}=\lambda^{-d}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}a_{i,j,k}\cdot\phi_{X}(x_{i})\cdot\phi_{Y}(y_{j})\cdot\phi_{Z}(z_{k})\right)+O(\lambda). $$

It is not hard to check that if $T^{\prime}\unrhd T$ , then $\tilde{R}(T^{\prime})\leq\tilde{R}(T)$ .

#### Restriction.

Restriction is a special type of degeneration that considers the case where the maps $\phi_{X},\phi_{Y},\phi_{Z}$ are $\mathbb{F}$ -linear maps. More specifically, $T^{\prime}$ is a restriction of $T$ if there exist $\mathbb{F}$ -linear maps

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{X} \displaystyle:\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}}(X)\to\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}}(X^{\prime}), \displaystyle\phi_{Y} \displaystyle:\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}}(Y)\to\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}}(Y^{\prime}), \displaystyle\phi_{Z} \displaystyle:\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}}(Z)\to\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}}(Z^{\prime}), $$

such that

$$ T^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}a_{i,j,k}\cdot\phi_{X}(x_{i})\cdot\phi_{Y}(y_{j})\cdot\phi_{Z}(z_{k}). $$

It is not hard to see that since the maps $\phi_{X},\phi_{Y},\phi_{Z}$ are linear transformations, we have $R(T^{\prime})\leq R(T)$ and consequently $\tilde{R}(T^{\prime})\leq\tilde{R}(T)$ .

#### Zero-out.

In the laser method, we only consider a limited type of restriction called zero-outs, namely the maps $\phi_{X},\phi_{Y},\phi_{Z}$ set some variables to zero. More specifically, we choose subsets $X^{\prime}\subseteq X$ , $Y^{\prime}\subseteq Y$ , $Z^{\prime}\subseteq Z$ and define the maps as

$$ \phi_{X}(x_{i})=\begin{cases}x_{i}&\text{If }x_{i}\in X^{\prime},\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} $$

and similarly for $\phi_{Y},\phi_{Z}$ . The resulting tensor

$$ T^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}a_{i,j,k}\cdot\phi_{X}(x_{i})\cdot\phi_{Y}(y_{j})\cdot\phi_{Z}(z_{k})=\sum_{x_{i}\in X^{\prime}}\sum_{y_{j}\in Y^{\prime}}\sum_{z_{k}\in Z^{\prime}}a_{i,j,k}\cdot x_{i}y_{j}z_{k} $$

is called a zero-out of $T$ . Throughout this paper, we use the notation $T^{\prime}=T|_{X^{\prime},Y^{\prime},Z^{\prime}}$ to denote such a tensor $T^{\prime}$ obtained as a zero-out of $T$ and we say that the variables in $X\setminus X^{\prime}$ , $Y\setminus Y^{\prime}$ , $Z\setminus Z^{\prime}$ are zeroed out. In this case, we also call $T^{\prime}$ the subtensor of $T$ over $X^{\prime},Y^{\prime},Z^{\prime}$ .

### 3.4 Matrix Multiplication Tensors

For positive integers $a,b,c$ , the $a\times b\times c$ matrix multiplication tensor $\langle a,b,c\rangle$ is a tensor over the variable sets $\{x_{ij}\}_{i\in[a],j\in[b]},\{y_{jk}\}_{j\in[b],k\in[c]},\{z_{ki}\}_{i\in[a],k\in[c]}$ defined as the tensor computing the $a\times c$ product matrix $\{z_{ki}\}_{i\in[a],k\in[c]}$ of an $a\times b$ matrix $\{x_{ij}\}_{i\in[a],j\in[b]}$ and $b\times c$ matrix $\{y_{jk}\}_{j\in[b],k\in[c]}$ . Specifically, $\langle a,b,c\rangle$ can be written as the trilinear form

$$ \langle a,b,c\rangle=\sum_{i\in[a]}\sum_{j\in[b]}\sum_{k\in[c]}x_{ij}y_{jk}z_{ki}. $$

It is not hard to check that $\langle a,b,c\rangle\otimes\langle d,e,f\rangle\equiv\langle ad,be,cf\rangle$ .

Following from the recursive approach introduced by Strassen in [strassen], for any integer $q\geq 2$ , if $R(\langle q,q,q\rangle)\leq r$ , then one can use the rank decomposition of $\langle q,q,q\rangle$ to design an arithmetic circuit of size $O(n^{\log_{q}(r)})$ to multiply two $n\times n$ matrices. This motivates the definition of the matrix multiplication exponent $\omega$ as follows:

$$ \omega:=\inf_{q\in\mathbb{N},\,q\geq 2}\log_{q}(R(\langle q,q,q\rangle)). $$

Namely, for every $\varepsilon>0$ , there exists an arithmetic circuit of size $O(n^{\omega+\varepsilon})$ that computes the multiplication of two $n\times n$ matrices. Since $\langle q,q,q\rangle^{\otimes n}\equiv\langle q^{n},q^{n},q^{n}\rangle$ , equivalently $\omega$ can be written in terms of the asymptotic rank of $\langle q,q,q\rangle$ as

$$ \omega=\log_{q}(\tilde{R}(\langle q,q,q\rangle)). $$

In this paper, we also consider the arithmetic complexity of multiplying rectangular matrices of sizes $n^{a}\times n^{b}$ and $n^{b}\times n^{c}$ where $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ . We define the quantity $\omega(a,b,c)$ similar to $\omega$ as

$$ \omega(a,b,c)=\log_{q}\left(\tilde{R}(\langle q^{a},q^{b},q^{c}\rangle)\right) $$

where $q\geq 2$ is a positive integer. This means that for any $\varepsilon>0$ , there exists an arithmetic circuit of size $O(n^{\omega(a,b,c)+\varepsilon})$ that computes the multiplication of an $n^{a}\times n^{b}$ matrix with an $n^{b}\times n^{c}$ matrix. In this paper, we focus on bounds for the values of the form $\omega(1,\kappa,1)$ for $\kappa>0$ . We remark that it is known that $\omega(1,1,\kappa)=\omega(1,\kappa,1)=\omega(\kappa,1,1)$ .

### 3.5 Schönhage’s Asymptotic Sum Inequality

By the above definition of $\omega$ , it is clear that if one can bound the asymptotic rank of matrix multiplication tensors, then one would get an upper bound on $\omega$ . In fact, Schönhage showed in [Schonhage81] that one can obtain an upper bound on $\omega$ if one can bound the asymptotic rank of a direct sum of matrix multiplication tensors. Specifically, we recall Shönhage’s asymptotic sum inequality as follows.

#### Theorem 3.1 (Asymptotic Sum Inequality [Schonhage81]).

For positive integers $r>m$ and $a_{i},b_{i},c_{i}$ for $i\in[m]$ , if

$$ \tilde{R}\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}\langle a_{i},b_{i},c_{i}\rangle\right)\leq r, $$

then $\omega\leq 3\tau$ where $\tau\in[2/3,1]$ is the solution to the equation

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{m}(a_{i}\cdot b_{i}\cdot c_{i})^{\tau}=r. $$

Analogously, the asymptotic sum inequality can also be used to obtain bounds on the rectangular matrix multiplication as follows.

#### Theorem 3.2 (Asymptotic Sum Inequality for $\omega(a,b,c)$ [Schonhage81]).

Let $t,\,q>0$ be positive integers and $a,b,c\geq 0$ , then

$$ t\cdot q^{\omega(a,b,c)}\leq\tilde{R}\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^{t}\langle q^{a},q^{b},q^{c}\rangle\right). $$

### 3.6 The Coppersmith-Winograd Tensor

For a nonnegative integer $q\geq 0$ , the Coppersmith-Winograd tensor $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ over the variables $X=\{x_{0},\dots,x_{q+1}\}$ , $Y=\{y_{0},\dots,y_{q+1}\}$ , $Z=\{z_{0},\dots,z_{q+1}\}$ is defined as

$$ \mathrm{CW}_{q}:=x_{0}y_{0}z_{q+1}+x_{0}y_{q+1}z_{0}+x_{q+1}y_{0}z_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{q}\left(x_{0}y_{i}z_{i}+x_{i}y_{0}z_{i}+x_{i}y_{i}z_{0}\right). $$

Observe that

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{q}x_{0}y_{i}z_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{q}x_{i}y_{0}z_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{q}x_{i}y_{i}z_{0}\equiv\langle 1,1,q\rangle+\langle q,1,1\rangle+\langle 1,q,1\rangle, $$

so $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ is the sum of six matrix multiplication tensors where the other three are copies of $\langle 1,1,1\rangle$ . It is known from Coppersmith and Winograd [cw90] that $\tilde{R}(\mathrm{CW}_{q})\leq q+2$ .

### 3.7 Base Leveled Partition of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$

We will consider the $2^{\ell-1}$ -th tensor power of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ for $\ell\geq 1$ . For convenience, we use the notation $T^{(\ell)}:=\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}$ . There is a natural partitioning of the variables of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ introduced in [cw90] and consequently used in all following works including [virgi12, AlmanW21, LeGall32power, duan2023]. We now describe the leveled partition of $T^{(\ell)}$ .

#### Level- $1$ Partition.

For $T^{(1)}=\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ , its variable sets $X^{(1)},Y^{(1)},Z^{(1)}$ are partitioned into three parts

$$ \displaystyle X^{(1)} \displaystyle=X^{(1)}_{0}\sqcup X^{(1)}_{1}\sqcup X^{(1)}_{2}=\{x_{0}\}\sqcup\{x_{1},\dots,x_{q}\}\sqcup\{x_{q+1}\}, \displaystyle Y^{(1)} \displaystyle=Y^{(1)}_{0}\sqcup Y^{(1)}_{1}\sqcup Y^{(1)}_{2}=\{y_{0}\}\sqcup\{y_{1},\dots,y_{q}\}\sqcup\{y_{q+1}\}, \displaystyle Z^{(1)} \displaystyle=Z^{(1)}_{0}\sqcup Z^{(1)}_{1}\sqcup Z^{(1)}_{2}=\{z_{0}\}\sqcup\{z_{1},\dots,z_{q}\}\sqcup\{z_{q+1}\}. $$

We use $T_{i,j,k}^{(1)}$ to denote the subtensor $T^{(1)}|_{X_{i},Y_{j},Z_{k}}$ and we call $T_{i,j,k}^{(1)}$ a level- $1$ constituent tensor. Then notice that under the above partition, the constituent tensor $T^{(1)}_{i,j,k}$ is nonzero if and only if $i+j+k=2$ . In particular, we can write $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ as a sum of constituent tensors as follows

$$ T^{(1)}=\mathrm{CW}_{q}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,k\geq 0\\
i+j+k=2\end{subarray}}T_{i,j,k}^{(1)}. $$

#### Level- $\ell$ Partition.

For $T^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}$ with variable sets $X^{(\ell)},Y^{(\ell)},Z^{(\ell)}$ , the above level- $1$ partition on $T^{(1)}$ directly induces a partition on the variable sets $X^{(\ell)},Y^{(\ell)},Z^{(\ell)}$ where each part of the partition is indexed by a $\{0,1,2\}$ -sequence of length $2^{\ell-1}$ . Specifically, this gives the partition

$$ X^{(\ell)}=\bigsqcup_{(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}}X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{1}}\otimes X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{2}}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}} $$

for $X$ -variables and analogous partitions for $Y$ - and $Z$ -variables.

In order to obtain an improvement by analyzing higher tensor powers of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ , we need to consider the following coarsening of the induced partition where the parts corresponding to sequences with the same sum are “merged” into a single part. More specifically, we have

$$ X^{(\ell)}=\bigsqcup_{i=0}^{2^{\ell}}X_{i}^{(\ell)},\qquad\textup{where}\quad X_{i}^{(\ell)}\coloneqq\bigsqcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}\\
\sum_{t}\hat{i}_{t}=i\end{subarray}}X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{1}}\otimes X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{2}}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}}. $$

We refer to this above coarsened partition of $T^{(\ell)}$ as the level- $\ell$ partition. Note that we can also view this partition as obtained from coarsening the level-( $\ell-1$ ) partition, i.e.,

$$ X_{i}^{(\ell)}=\bigsqcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq i^{\prime}\leq i\\
0\leq i^{\prime},i-i^{\prime}\leq 2^{\ell}\end{subarray}}X^{(\ell-1)}_{i^{\prime}}\otimes X^{(\ell-1)}_{i-i^{\prime}}. $$

We can partition the variable sets $Y^{(\ell)}$ and $Z^{(\ell)}$ similarly.

Under the level- $\ell$ partition, we use $T^{(\ell)}_{i,j,k}$ to denote the subtensor $T^{(\ell)}|_{X_{i}^{(\ell)},Y_{j}^{(\ell)},Z_{k}^{(\ell)}}$ and note that $T^{(\ell)}_{i,j,k}$ is nonzero if and only if $i+j+k=2^{\ell}$ . So we have

$$ T^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,k\geq 0\\
i+j+k=2^{\ell}\end{subarray}}T_{i,j,k}^{(\ell)}. $$

We call each $T^{(\ell)}_{i,j,k}$ a level- $\ell$ constituent tensor, $X^{(\ell)}_{i},Y^{(\ell)}_{j},Z^{(\ell)}_{k}$ level- $\ell$ variable blocks, and we omit the superscript $(\ell)$ when $\ell$ is clear from context.

### 3.8 Leveled Partition for Large Tensor Powers of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$

In the laser method, we consider a large tensor power of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ in the form $(T^{(\ell)})^{\otimes n}=(\mathrm{CW}_{q})^{\otimes n\cdot 2^{\ell-1}}$ . We set $N:=n\cdot 2^{\ell-1}$ and note that the leveled partition of $T^{(\ell)}$ induces a partition on $(T^{\ell})^{\otimes n}$ . We recall some basic terminology and notations with respect to the leveled-partition of $(T^{\ell})^{\otimes n}$ .

#### Level- $1$ partition of $(\mathrm{CW}_{q})^{\otimes N}$ .

In level- $1$ , we view $(\mathrm{CW}_{q})^{\otimes N}$ as the tensor $(T^{(1)})^{\otimes N}$ and consider the partition induced by the level- $1$ partition on $T^{(1)}$ . Each level- $1$ $X$ -variable block $X_{\hat{I}}$ is indexed by a sequence $\hat{I}=(\hat{I}_{1},\dots,\hat{I}_{N})$ of length $N$ in $\{0,1,2\}^{N}$ . The variable block $X_{I}$ is defined as

$$ X_{\hat{I}}:=X_{\hat{I}_{1}}^{(1)}\otimes\dots\otimes X_{\hat{I}_{N}}^{(1)}, $$

where $X_{I_{t}}^{(1)}$ for $t\in[N]$ is the level- $1$ partition of $T^{(1)}$ . We call $X_{\hat{I}}$ a level- $1$ variable block and $\hat{I}$ its level- $1$ index sequence. The level- $1$ $Y$ - and $Z$ -variable blocks $Y_{\hat{J}}$ and $Z_{\hat{K}}$ are defined similarly for level- $1$ index sequences $\hat{J},\hat{K}\in\{0,1,2\}^{N}$ . Then notice that $X_{\hat{I}},Y_{\hat{J}},Z_{\hat{K}}$ form a nonzero subtensor of $(T^{(1)})^{\otimes N}$ if $\hat{I}_{t}+\hat{J}_{t}+\hat{K}_{t}=2$ for all $t\in[N]$ . So we can write $(T^{(1)})^{\otimes N}$ as a sum of subtensors

$$ (T^{(1)})^{\otimes N}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\hat{I},\hat{J},\hat{K}\in\{0,1,2\}^{N}\\
\hat{I}_{t}+\hat{J}_{t}+\hat{K}_{t}=2\,\ \forall t\in[N]\end{subarray}}(T^{(1)})^{\otimes N}\big|_{X_{\hat{I}},Y_{\hat{J}},Z_{\hat{K}}}. $$

For convenience, we use $X_{\hat{I}}Y_{\hat{J}}Z_{\hat{K}}$ to denote the subtensor $(T^{(1)})^{\otimes N}|_{X_{\hat{I}},Y_{\hat{J}},Z_{\hat{K}}}$ and we call $X_{\hat{I}}Y_{\hat{J}}Z_{\hat{K}}$ a level- $1$ triple.

#### Level- $\ell$ partition of $(\mathrm{CW}_{q})^{\otimes N}$ .

In level- $\ell$ , we view $(\mathrm{CW}_{q})^{\otimes N}$ as the tensor $(T^{(\ell)})^{\otimes n}$ where $n=N/2^{\ell-1}$ and consider the partition induced by the level- $\ell$ partition on $T^{(\ell)}$ . Each level- $1$ $X$ -variable block $X_{I}$ is indexed by a sequence $I\in\{0,1,\dots,2^{\ell}\}^{n}$ of length $n$ . The variable block $X_{I}$ is defined as

$$ X_{I}:=X_{I_{1}}^{(\ell)}\otimes\dots\otimes X_{I_{n}}^{(\ell)} $$

where $X_{i}^{(\ell)}$ ( $0\leq i\leq 2^{\ell}$ ) is the $i$ -th part in the level- $\ell$ partition of $T^{(\ell)}$ . We call $X_{I}$ a level- $\ell$ variable block and $I$ its level- $\ell$ index sequence. The level- $\ell$ $Y$ - and $Z$ -variable blocks $Y_{J}$ and $Z_{K}$ are defined similarly for level- $\ell$ index sequences $J,K\in\{0,1,\dots,2^{\ell}\}^{n}$ . Similarly, the level- $\ell$ variable blocks $X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K}$ form a nonzero subtensor of $(T^{(\ell)})^{\otimes n}$ when $I_{t}+J_{t}+K_{t}=2^{\ell}$ for all $t\in[n]$ . So we can write

$$ (T^{(\ell)})^{\otimes n}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\hat{I},\hat{J},\hat{K}\in\{0,1,2^{\ell}\}^{n}\\
I_{t}+J_{t}+K_{t}=2^{\ell}\,\ \forall t\in[N]\end{subarray}}(T^{(\ell)})^{\otimes n}|_{X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K}}. $$

For convenience, we use the notation $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ to denote the subtensor $(T^{(\ell)})^{\otimes n}|_{X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K}}$ and we call such $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ a level- $\ell$ triple.

In addition, note that since the level- $\ell$ partition of $T^{(\ell)}$ is a coarsening of the partition induced by the level- $1$ partition of $T^{(1)}$ , a level- $1$ variable block $X_{\hat{I}}$ is contained in a level- $\ell$ variable block $X_{I}$ if the sequence $I^{\prime}=(I^{\prime}_{1},\dots,I^{\prime}_{n})$ formed by taking $I^{\prime}_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{2^{\ell-1}}\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+i}$ satisfies $I^{\prime}_{t}=I_{t}$ for all $t\in[n]$ . Namely, if taking the sum of consecutive length- $2^{\ell-1}$ subsequences in $\hat{I}$ yields the sequence $I$ , then $X_{\hat{I}}$ is contained in $X_{I}$ . In this case, we use the notation $\hat{I}\in I$ and $X_{\hat{I}}\in X_{I}$ .

### 3.9 Distributions and Entropy

In this paper, we only consider distributions with a finite support. Let $\alpha$ be a distribution supported on a set $S$ , we have $\alpha(s)\geq 0$ for all $s\in S$ and $\sum_{s\in S}\alpha(s)=1$ . The entropy of $\alpha$ , denoted as $H(\alpha)$ , is defined as

$$ H(\alpha)\coloneqq-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in S\\
\alpha(s)>0\end{subarray}}\alpha(s)\log\alpha(s), $$

where the $\log$ has base $2$ . We will frequently use the following well-known combinatorial fact.

#### Lemma 3.3.

Let $\alpha$ be a distribution over the set $[s]=\{1,\dots,s\}$ . Let $N>0$ be a positive integer, then we have

$$ \binom{N}{\alpha(1)N,\dots,\alpha(s)N}=2^{N(H(\alpha)\pm o(1))}. $$

For two distributions $\alpha$ and $\beta$ over the sets $S$ and $S^{\prime}$ respectively, we define the joint distribution $\alpha\times\beta$ as the distribution over $S\times S^{\prime}=\{(s,s^{\prime})\mid s\in S,s^{\prime}\in S^{\prime}\}$ such that

$$ (\alpha\times\beta)(s,s^{\prime})=\alpha(s)\cdot\beta(s^{\prime}). $$

When $S$ and $S^{\prime}$ are sets of integer sequences, we will instead define $\alpha\times\beta$ as a distribution over all integer sequences that can be obtained by concatenating one sequence in $S$ and one sequence in $S^{\prime}$ , such that

$$ (\alpha\times\beta)(s\circ s^{\prime})=\alpha(s)\cdot\beta(s^{\prime}), $$

where $s\circ s^{\prime}$ denotes the concatenation of $s$ and $s^{\prime}$ .

### 3.10 Complete Split Distributions

Motivated by the leveled partition of tensor powers of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ , we define the notion of complete split distributions to characterize the level- $1$ variable blocks contained in level- $\ell$ variable blocks.

#### Definition 3.4 (Complete Split Distribution).

A complete split distribution for a level- $\ell$ constituent tensor $T_{i,j,k}$ with $i+j+k=2^{\ell}$ is a distribution on all length $2^{\ell-1}$ sequences $(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ .

For a level- $1$ index sequence $\hat{I}\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}\cdot n}$ , we say that it is consistent with a complete split distribution $\beta$ if the proportion of any index sequence $(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})$ in

$$ \left\{\bigl(\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+p}\bigr)_{p=1}^{2^{\ell-1}}\;\middle|\;t\in[n]\right\} $$

equals $\beta(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})$ . Namely, for every $(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ , we have

$$ \left\lvert\left\{t\in[n]\;\middle|\;\bigl(\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+p}\bigr)_{p=1}^{2^{\ell-1}}=(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\right\}\right\rvert=\beta(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\cdot n. $$

Notice that any level-1 index sequence $\hat{I}\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}\cdot n}$ defines a complete split distribution by computing the proportions of each type of length- $2^{\ell-1}$ consecutive chunks present in $\hat{I}$ . More specifically, we have the following definition.

#### Definition 3.5.

Given a level-1 index sequence $\hat{I}\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}\cdot n}$ , its complete split distribution over $(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ is defined as

$$ \textsf{{split}}\bigl(\hat{I}\bigr)\bigl(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)=\frac{1}{n}\cdot\left\lvert\left\{t\in[n]\;\middle|\;\bigl(\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+p}\bigr)_{p=1}^{2^{\ell-1}}=\bigl(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)\right\}\right\rvert. $$

Given a subset $S\subseteq[n]$ , we can define the complete split distribution over $(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ given by $\hat{I}$ restricted to the subset $S$ as

$$ \textsf{{split}}\bigl(\hat{I},S\bigr)\bigl(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)=\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot\left\lvert\left\{t\in S\;\middle|\;\bigl(\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+p}\bigr)_{p=1}^{2^{\ell-1}}=\bigl(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)\right\}\right\rvert. $$

Given two complete split distributions $\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}$ over the length- $2^{\ell-1}$ index sequences $\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ , the $L_{\infty}$ distances between $\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}$ is defined to be

$$ \left\lVert\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}\right\rVert_{\infty}=\max_{\sigma\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}}|\beta_{1}(\sigma)-\beta_{2}(\sigma)|. $$

For any constant $\varepsilon>0$ and a fixed complete split distribution $\beta$ , we say that a level-1 index sequence $\hat{I}\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}\cdot n}$ is consistent with $\beta$ up to $\varepsilon$ error if $\lVert\textsf{{split}}(\hat{I})-\beta\rVert_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon$ . When the $\varepsilon$ is clear from context, we say that $\hat{I}$ is approximately consistent with $\beta$ if it is consistent with $\beta$ up to $\varepsilon$ error.

#### Definition 3.6.

For a level- $\ell$ constituent tensor $T_{i,j,k}$ , an integer exponent $N$ , a constant $\varepsilon\geq 0$ , and three complete split distributions $\beta_{X},\beta_{Y},\beta_{Z}$ for the $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variables respectively, we define

$$ T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes N}[\beta_{X},\beta_{Y},\beta_{Z},\varepsilon]:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{level-}1\text{ triple }X_{\hat{I}}Y_{\hat{J}}Z_{\hat{K}}\textup{ in }T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes N}\\
\hat{I}\text{ approximately consistent with }\beta_{X}\\
\hat{J}\text{ approximately consistent with }\beta_{Y}\\
\hat{K}\text{ approximately consistent with }\beta_{Z}\end{subarray}}X_{\hat{I}}Y_{\hat{J}}Z_{\hat{K}}. $$

It is a subtensor of $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes N}$ over all level-1 $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variable blocks that are approximately consistent with $\beta_{\textit{X}}$ , $\beta_{\textit{Y}}$ , $\beta_{\textit{Z}}$ , respectively. When $\varepsilon=0$ , we will simplify the notation to $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes N}[\beta_{X},\beta_{Y},\beta_{Z}]$ .

### 3.11 Salem-Spencer Sets

In the hashing step of the laser method, we make use of the existence of a large dense subset of $\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ that avoids $3$ -term arithmetic progressions. We recall the following past result.

#### Theorem 3.7 ([salemspencer, behrend1946sets]).

For every positive integer $M>0$ , there exists a subset $B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ of size

$$ |B|\geq M\cdot e^{-O(\sqrt{\log M})}=M^{1-o(1)} $$

that contains no nontrivial $3$ -term arithmetic progressions. Specifically, any $a,b,c\in B$ satisfy $a+b\equiv 2c\pmod{M}$ if and only if $a=b=c$ .

## 4 Algorithm Outline

In the following, we will use $\kappa\geq 0$ to denote that we want to obtain an upper bound on $\omega(1,\kappa,1)$ .

In this section, we give the outline of our algorithm, which accepts $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes N}$ as its input for a large enough $N$ , and degenerates it into a collection of independent matrix multiplication tensors of the same size $\left\langle m,m^{\kappa},m\right\rangle$ . By the asymptotic sum inequality (Theorem 3.2), this will give an upper bound on $\omega(1,\kappa,1)$ .

### 4.1 Algorithm Framework

The following notion of interface tensor acts as an interface of our algorithm between different levels. In general, each level of our algorithm takes an interface tensor as input (except the first level, which takes a large tensor power of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ ), and degenerates it into independent copies of an interface tensor.

#### Definition 4.1 (Interface Tensor).

For a positive integer $\ell\geq 1$ and any constant $0\leq\varepsilon\leq 1$ , a level- $\ell$ $\varepsilon$ -interface tensor $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ with parameter list

$$ \{(n_{t},i_{t},j_{t},k_{t},\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t})\}_{t\in[s]} $$

is defined as

$$ \mathcal{T}^{*}\coloneqq\bigotimes_{t=1}^{s}T_{i_{t},j_{t},k_{t}}^{\otimes n_{t}}[\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t},\varepsilon], $$

where $i_{t}+j_{t}+k_{t}=2^{\ell}$ for every $t\in[s]$ (i.e., $T_{i_{t},j_{t},k_{t}}$ is a level- $\ell$ constituent tensor) and $\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t}$ are level- $\ell$ complete split distributions for $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variables respectively. We call each $T_{i_{t},j_{t},k_{t}}^{\otimes n_{t}}[\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t},\varepsilon]$ a term of $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ . When $\varepsilon=0$ , we will simply call $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ a level- $\ell$ interface tensor.

Note that the same $(i_{t},j_{t},k_{t})$ can appear multiple times in the parameter list, with potentially different $n_{k},\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t}$ . Also note that the tensor product of two level- $\ell$ $\varepsilon$ -interface tensors is also a level- $\ell$ $\varepsilon$ -interface tensor, whose parameter list is the concatenation of the parameter lists of the two level- $\ell$ $\varepsilon$ -interface tensors.

The framework of our algorithm is as follows. First, we apply the global stage algorithm described in Section 5 on input $\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell^{*}}}\bigr)^{\otimes n}$ to degenerate it into independent copies of a level- $\ell^{*}$ $\varepsilon_{\ell^{*}}$ -interface tensor. Then we apply the constituent tensor stage algorithm described in Section 6 for $\ell=\ell^{*},\ell^{*}-1,\dots,2$ to obtain the tensor product between a matrix multiplication tensor and independent copies of a level- $1$ $\varepsilon_{1}$ -interface tensor. More specifically, the constituent tensor stage algorithm takes as input a level- $\ell$ $\varepsilon_{\ell}$ -interface tensor and outputs the tensor product between a matrix multiplication tensor and independent copies of a level- $(\ell-1)$ $\varepsilon_{\ell-1}$ -interface tensor, so we can keep applying the constituent tensor stage algorithm on each level- $(\ell-1)$ interface tensors that was outputted previously until we get a tensor product between a matrix multiplication tensor and independent copies of a level- $1$ $\varepsilon_{1}$ -interface tensor. Finally, we show that each level- $1$ $\varepsilon_{1}$ -interface tensor can be easily degenerated into a matrix multiplication tensor, so we obtain independent copies of matrix multiplication tensors of dimension $\left\langle m,m^{\kappa},m\right\rangle$ .

### 4.2 Algorithm Outline

We first give a high-level outline of each step of the global stage algorithm. The constituent tensor stage algorithm will share similar high-level ideas.

The algorithm takes in $\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes n}$ as input and outputs level- $1$ -independent level- $\ell$ interface tensors as a degeneration of the input (for simplicity, we consider the $\varepsilon=0$ case in this outline). In the algorithm, we define the notion of compatibility between level- $1$ blocks and level- $\ell$ triples with respect to some specified complete split distributions, so that if all level- $1$ blocks in the remaining tensor are compatible with exactly one level- $\ell$ triple, then the subtensors over each remaining triple are level- $1$ -independent. So the goal of the algorithm is to zero out some level- $\ell$ and level- $1$ variable blocks such that each remaining level- $1$ block is compatible with a unique level- $\ell$ triple. The structure of the algorithm is similar to the global stage algorithm in [duan2023] with the main modification being the generalization from split distributions to complete split distributions.

On input $\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes n}$ , we first view the tensor as the tensor product of three terms, where each term is called a region, i.e., we write $\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes n}$ as $\bigotimes_{r\in[3]}\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes A_{r}\cdot n}$ for some $A_{1},A_{2},A_{3}\geq 0$ and $A_{1}+A_{2}+A_{3}=1$ . Recall that we are only able to allow the sharing of level- $\ell$ variable blocks in one of $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -dimensions, so each region will allow the sharing of level- $\ell$ variable blocks in different dimensions and we will perform the subsequent steps on the three regions separately. This step helps balance the number of remaining variable blocks in the three dimensions due to the asymmetric nature of the subsequent procedure.

From now on, we describe the procedure on the first region where we allow the sharing of level- $\ell$ $Z$ -variable blocks. We perform the same procedure up to rotation of the three dimensions on the other two regions separately.

- 1. Zero out according to $\alpha$ . For a distribution $\alpha$ over the level- $\ell$ constituent subtensors and its induced marginals ${\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}$ in the $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -dimensions, we zero out level- $\ell$ $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variable blocks that are not consistent with ${\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}$ respectively.

- 2. Asymmetric hashing. We use pairwise independent hash functions that hash level- $\ell$ index sequences to the set $\{0,\dots,M-1\}$ for some $M$ which partitions the level- $\ell$ variable blocks into buckets based on its hash value. Within each bucket, we do asymmetric cleanup so that every level- $\ell$ $X$ -variable block $X_{I}$ or $Y$ -variable block $Y_{J}$ is contained in a unique level- $\ell$ triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ , while a level- $\ell$ $Z$ -variable block $Z_{K}$ could be contained in multiple level- $\ell$ triples.

- 3. Compatibility zero-out I. We define a notion of compatibility with respect to the complete split distributions between level- $1$ blocks and level- $\ell$ triples for a set of specified level- $\ell$ complete split distributions $\left\{\beta_{X,i,j,k},\beta_{Y,i,j,k},\beta_{Z,i,j,k}\right\}_{i+j+k=2^{\ell}}$ for the $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -blocks. We zero out all the level- $1$ $X$ - or $Y$ -blocks that are not consistent with $\left\{\beta_{X,i,j,k}\right\}_{i+j+k=2^{\ell}},\left\{\beta_{Y,i,j,k}\right\}_{i+j+k=2^{\ell}}$ respectively (we can only do this because every level- $\ell$ $X$ -variable block $X_{I}$ or $Y$ -variable block $Y_{J}$ is contained in a unique level- $\ell$ triple). We zero out all the level- $1$ $Z$ -blocks that are incompatible with any level- $\ell$ triples.

- 4. Compatibility zero-out II: unique triple. After the compatibility zero-out I, every level- $1$ block is compatible with at least $1$ level- $\ell$ triple and we want every level- $1$ block to be compatible with exactly one level- $\ell$ triple. So in this step, we zero out level-1 $Z$ -blocks that are compatible with more than one level- $\ell$ triples. Note that the level- $1$ blocks zeroed out in this step will become holes.

- 5. Usefulness zero-out. Now that each remaining level- $1$ $Z$ -block $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is contained in exactly one level- $\ell$ triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ , we can define the notion of whether a level- $1$ block is useful for the level- $\ell$ triple containing it as whether it is consistent with the complete split distributions $\{\beta_{Z,i,j,k}\}_{i+j+k=2^{\ell}}$ . Note that we can only do this now because previously we do not have the property that every level- $1$ $Z$ -block is in a unique level- $\ell$ triple. In this step we zero out the level- $1$ blocks that are not useful for the level- $\ell$ triple containing it.

- 6. Fixing holes. Now we have obtained level-1-independent level- $\ell$ interface tensors with holes. We use the following result which will be proved in Section 7 to fix the holes. Corollary 4.2 (Fixing holes in interface tensors). Let $T$ be a level- $\ell$ interface tensor with parameter list

$$ \{(n_{t},i_{t},j_{t},k_{t},\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t})\}_{t\in[s]}. $$

Let $N=2^{\ell-1}\cdot\sum_{t\in[s]}n_{t}$ . Suppose $T_{1},\dots,T_{r}$ are broken copies of $T$ where $\leq\frac{1}{8N}$ fraction of level-1 $X$ -, $Y$ - and $Z$ -blocks are holes. If $r\geq 2^{C_{1}N/\log N}$ for some large enough constant $C_{1}>0$ , the direct sum $\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}T_{i}$ can degenerate into an unbroken copy of $T$ .

Similar to [duan2023], we consider
